ap_physics_c_mechanics-f01.title: Block sliding down a rough incline

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=2\text{ kg}$ is released from rest at the top of a rough incline that makes an angle of $\theta=40^\circ$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is $\mu=0.15$. The block slides a distance $d=4\text{ m}$ along the incline. Use $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the block, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the block while it slides down the incline. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Three arrows from the dot: weight straight down, the normal force perpendicular to the incline, and kinetic friction directed up the incline (opposite to the motion).

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the weight, the normal force and the friction force, with no extra force such as a force of motion
common_errors: adds a force down the incline

rubric_rows.criterion: The weight points straight down and the normal force is perpendicular to the surface of the incline
common_errors: draws the normal force vertical

rubric_rows.criterion: The friction force points up the incline, opposite to the direction of the motion
common_errors: draws friction down the incline

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed $v$ of the block after it has slid the distance $d$, in terms of $g$, $d$, $\theta$ and $\mu$.
parts.model_answer: $N=mg\cos\theta$ and $f=\mu mg\cos\theta$. The work-energy theorem gives $mgd\sin\theta-\mu mgd\cos\theta=\tfrac12mv^2$, so $v=\sqrt{2gd(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the normal force $N=mg\cos\theta$ and the friction force $f=\mu mg\cos\theta$
required_elements: f = mu m g cos theta
common_errors: uses N = m g

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies the work-energy theorem with the work of the weight component and of friction: $mgd\sin\theta-fd=\tfrac12mv^2$
required_elements: m g d sin theta - f d = 1/2 m v^2
common_errors: omits the work of friction

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v=\sqrt{2gd(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)}$
required_elements: sqrt(2 g d (sin theta - mu cos theta))
common_errors: obtains $\sqrt{2gd(\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta)}$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the block after it has slid $4\text{ m}$ for $\theta=40^\circ$ and $\mu=0.15$.
parts.model_answer: $v=\sqrt{2(9.8)(4)(\sin40^\circ-0.15\cos40^\circ)}\approx 6.43\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes the values into the expression from part B
common_errors: uses the cosine and the sine interchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 6.43 with units of meters per second

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The coefficient of kinetic friction is doubled to $0.3$ with everything else unchanged. Does the speed of the block after sliding $4\text{ m}$ increase, decrease or stay the same, and what is its new value? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It decreases, because a larger friction force removes more energy over the same distance: $v=\sqrt{2gd(\sin\theta-2\mu\cos\theta)}\approx5.69\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the speed decreases and gives about 5.69 with units of meters per second
common_errors: states that the speed is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the work done by friction, $\mu mgd\cos\theta$, is larger, so less of the gravitational energy becomes kinetic energy
common_errors: argues only that friction is bigger without relating it to the energy

stimulus.description: A student wraps a light string around the rim of a horizontal disk of radius R = 0.1 m that rotates on a frictionless axle. A mass m hangs from the string and is released from rest. The student measures the acceleration a of the hanging mass for several values of m and wants to determine the rotational inertia I of the disk. Assume the string does not slip.

data.y_label: Acceleration of the hanging mass a (m/s^2)
notes: A student wraps a light string around the rim of a horizontal disk of radius R = 0.1 m that rotates on a frictionless axle. A mass m hangs from the string and is released from rest. The student measures the acceleration a of the hanging mass for several values of m and wants to determine the rotational inertia I of the disk. Assume the string does not slip.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the acceleration as a function of the hanging mass. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the independent variable is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the measured acceleration.
parts.model_answer: Measure each hanging mass with a balance; release it from rest and measure the distance it falls with a meterstick and the fall time with a stopwatch (or a photogate) to find $a=2h/t^2$; change only the hanging mass with the same disk, string and release height; reduce the uncertainty by repeating each release and averaging the times or by using a larger fall height.

ap_physics_c_mechanics-f04.title: Skater pulling in her arms

stimulus.description: A figure skater spins about a vertical axis on frictionless ice with her arms extended. Her rotational inertia is $I_i=4\text{ kg·m}^2$ and her angular speed is $\omega_i=1.5\text{ rad/s}$. She then pulls her arms in so that her rotational inertia becomes $I_f=1.6\text{ kg·m}^2$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that the kinetic energy of the skater does not change when she pulls her arms in, because angular momentum is conserved. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. Angular momentum is conserved because no external torque acts, but the rotational kinetic energy $K=L^2/(2I)$ increases when $I$ decreases at constant $L$; the energy comes from the work done by the skater's muscles.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim
common_errors: agrees because both are conserved

common_errors: says that both quantities are conserved in every interaction

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the final angular speed $\omega_f$ in terms of $I_i$, $I_f$ and $\omega_i$, and calculate its value.
parts.model_answer: $I_i\omega_i=I_f\omega_f$ gives $\omega_f=I_i\omega_i/I_f=3.75\text{ rad/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies conservation of angular momentum: $I_i\omega_i=I_f\omega_f$
common_errors: conserves the kinetic energy instead

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $\omega_f=I_i\omega_i/I_f$
common_errors: inverts the ratio of the rotational inertias

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $\omega_f$ of about 3.75 with units of radians per second

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the ratio of her final rotational kinetic energy to her initial rotational kinetic energy, and state which agent does the work that changes the energy.
parts.model_answer: $K_f/K_i=(\tfrac12I_f\omega_f^2)/(\tfrac12I_i\omega_i^2)=I_i/I_f=2.50$; the extra energy comes from the work done by the skater's muscles in pulling the arms inward.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates a kinetic energy ratio of about 2.50
common_errors: gives a ratio less than one
